t: Aim and plan of the session
n: This is laboratory session no. 7. In it we analyse methyl, ethyl and amyl alcohols in the second distillate by chemical methods. The plan: analysis of methyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol and amyl alcohol in the distillate by chemical methods. The aim: students must know the toxicological and narcological significance of the alcohols and their dosage forms, and master the analysis of distillates.

As a result of the session the student analyses methyl, ethyl and amyl alcohols in the distillate by chemical methods. The work requires the distillate, flasks, test tubes, reagents, demonstration materials, adhesive tape and paper. The session takes place in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities.

The methods for isolating alcohols from the object differ. Methyl alcohol distils well with water; up to 32% of the alcohol is lost in distillation, so dephlegmation is used to raise its concentration. Ethyl alcohol is also steam-distilled; when drunk it passes quickly into the blood, and it can be detected in the blood after 5 minutes. Amyl alcohol is distilled from the object with steam, and to increase sensitivity the distillate is extracted with ether. Ethylene glycol, by contrast, distils poorly with steam, so it is isolated by the method of Lapkina and Nazarenko.

Methyl alcohol is widely used in the chemical industry: chiefly as a raw material for the synthesis of formaldehyde and as a solvent for varnishes and nitro paints. It is also used in pharmacy and agriculture. Pure methyl alcohol is a mobile, colourless, clear liquid; it mixes well with water and organic solvents, and its odour resembles ethyl alcohol. Poisoning occurs as a result of methyl alcohol being used in place of ethyl alcohol.

The significance of methyl alcohol. It has a strong effect on the human body; poisoning occurs as a result of its use in place of ethyl alcohol. The toxic dose is 7-8 g, LD50 = 30-100 g. It is a neurotoxic substance that accumulates in the body. The poisoned person loses consciousness and may die; some survivors lose their sight. In the corpse, haemorrhages in the internal organs, congestion of the brain, and fatty infiltration of the liver and spleen are observed; the urine contains a great deal of formic acid.

The metabolism of methyl alcohol. In the body, methyl alcohol is oxidised to formaldehyde and then to formic acid. This is why the urine of the corpse contains a great deal of formic acid. Formic acid is then further oxidised to carbonic acid, that is, to CO2 and water.

We detect methyl alcohol by the ester formation reaction. 1 ml of distillate, or aqueous solution, is mixed with crystals of salicylic acid. Then 3-4 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid is added and the mixture is heated. The characteristic pleasant odour of methyl salicylate is perceived.

t: Essence of the methyl salicylate reaction
n: The essence of the methyl salicylate reaction. In the presence of concentrated H2SO4, methyl alcohol forms with salicylic acid methyl salicylate, an ester with a distinctive odour. If there is no ethyl alcohol in the distillate, the odour formed is characteristic of methyl alcohol. But ethyl alcohol also gives this reaction, and the odours are similar; for this reason the reaction is of limited use.

t: Methyl alcohol: oxidation and detection of formaldehyde
n: Oxidation of methyl alcohol and detection of the formaldehyde formed. To 5 ml of distillate, 2-3 ml of 10% sulphuric acid is added and the mixture is cooled; 1% KMnO4 is added dropwise until a stable pale violet colour. The mixture is left for 15-20 minutes in a cool place. Excess permanganate is removed with 15% oxalic acid. With the filtrate, reactions 2 and 3 for formaldehyde given above, that is, the codeine and fuchsin-sulphurous acid reactions, are carried out.

t: Equation for the oxidation of methyl alcohol
n: The equation for the oxidation of methyl alcohol. Methyl alcohol is oxidised by potassium permanganate and sulphuric acid to form formaldehyde. Excess permanganate is removed with oxalic acid. The formaldehyde formed is detected with fuchsin-sulphurous acid. The reaction proceeds in a cold medium over 15-20 minutes.

The significance of ethyl alcohol. By its pharmacological action it belongs to the group of narcotic substances: first excitation, then a state of narcosis occurs, and regular consumption leads to alcoholism. The addition of chloral hydrate, cocaine, opium alkaloids or barbiturates to alcoholic drinks is the cause of many deaths. In poisoning, the concentration of alcohol in the urine is considerably higher than in the blood. In the body it is rapidly oxidised in the liver, 90-99% to CO2. The stomach, liver, kidneys and brain may be taken for analysis; 100-300 g of alcohol is fatal.

The properties and metabolism of ethyl alcohol. Pure ethyl alcohol is a mobile, colourless, volatile liquid with a burning taste; it mixes well with water and ether, and boils at 77-78.5 °C. It burns with a bluish flame, is steam-distilled, and is readily oxidised to form acetaldehyde. In the body it is rapidly oxidised in the liver: 90-99% to CO2, and the rest is excreted through the breath and the kidneys.

Signs of ethyl alcohol poisoning. When alcohol is drunk, the nervous system is first excited and then quickly replaced by a state of narcosis; regular consumption leads to alcoholism. The addition of chloral hydrate, cocaine, opium alkaloids and barbiturates to drinks is the cause of many deaths. In intoxication, vomit may block the airway and lead to death. The internal organs of the corpse smell of alcohol.

The iodoform reaction for ethyl alcohol. To 1 ml of distillate, 1 ml of 1% alkali is added, then a solution of iodine in KI is added dropwise until a pale yellow colour. The mixture is heated on a water bath at 50 °C: the odour of iodoform is perceived, and if there is a lot, a yellow precipitate forms. Under the microscope, hexagonal star-shaped microcrystals are seen; their shape is drawn in the laboratory notebook.

The chemical essence of the iodoform reaction. In an alkaline medium, ethyl alcohol is oxidised by iodine to acetaldehyde, which is converted into iodoform. Iodoform is a yellow turbidity with a distinctive odour; under the microscope, six-sided yellow star-shaped crystals are seen. Remember: the reaction has negative significance, because substances with the corresponding group are common in the body.

After iodoform has formed, if 1 drop of aniline is added to the liquid and it is heated, isonitrile with a foul odour is formed. To detect acetaldehyde, 1 ml of distillate is mixed with 1 ml of 10% H2SO4, and 10% potassium dichromate is added until a brownish-yellow colour. After the mixture has stood briefly at room temperature, the characteristic odour of acetaldehyde is perceived. Here the ethyl alcohol is oxidised by the dichromate and a green colour appears.

t: Ethyl alcohol: ethyl acetate and quantity
n: We also detect ethyl alcohol through ethyl acetate. To 1 ml of distillate, crystals of sodium acetate are added, followed by H2SO4 at double concentration. The mixture is heated on a water bath until air bubbles form. If ethyl alcohol is present, the odour of acetic ethyl ester is perceived; if the mixture is poured into 20-25 ml of cold water, the odour is distinct. The quantity is determined by the ethyl nitrite, Widmark-Shaymosh, Karantaev (photoelectrocolorimetry, PEC) and GLC methods.

The quantity of ethyl alcohol is determined by four methods: the ethyl nitrite method, the Widmark-Shaymosh method, the Karantaev method (PEC) and GLC. The Karantaev method is photocolorimetric, and GLC is gas-liquid chromatography. Ethyl alcohol is oxidised quickly, so the analysis must be carried out without delay. The stomach, liver, kidneys and brain may be taken for analysis.

The ester-forming reactions of ethyl alcohol. If concentrated H2SO4 and a crystal of CH3COONa are added to the distillate and the mixture is heated, the odour of acetic ethyl ester is perceived. In an alkaline medium, benzoyl chloride forms with ethyl alcohol an ester with a distinctive odour. An alkaline solution of iodine gives iodoform; if aniline is added after the iodoform, isonitrile forms and a foul odour is perceived. The quantity of ethyl alcohol is determined by the ethyl nitrite, Widmark-Shaymosh, Karantaev (PEC) and GLC methods.

The significance and isolation of amyl alcohol. Amyl alcohol is often present in samogon, that is, home-made vodka prepared from sugar. Amyl and isoamyl alcohols act on the central nervous system; 10-15 g of amyl alcohol is fatal. Before analysis the distillate is extracted with ether; the ether is passed through a dry filter and divided equally among four porcelain dishes. The ether is evaporated at room temperature, and the reactions are carried out on the residues.

The course of amyl alcohol poisoning. Amyl alcohol acts within 20-30 minutes and brings rapid intoxication, but then sudden loss of consciousness occurs. Cyanosis, that is, bluish discoloration of the skin, develops; after 10-15 minutes death occurs in convulsions. Amyl alcohol is absorbed very slowly in the body, and the unabsorbed portion remains in the stomach, which is essential for forensic chemical analysis. In the corpse, asphyxia and an odour of alcohol are observed.

The properties and uses of amyl alcohol. Amyl and isoamyl alcohol form a yellowish, viscous liquid with a sharp, suffocating odour; poorly soluble in water, readily soluble in organic solvents. The undissolved part floats on the water; if there is a lot, an oily liquid forms on the surface of the distillate. It is used as a solvent in the varnish and paint industry, and in making amyl nitrite, valerian acid preparations and smokeless powder.

The salicylaldehyde reaction for amyl alcohol. To the residue in the first dish, 20-25 drops of 1% salicylaldehyde and 3 ml of concentrated H2SO4 are added. When the mixture has cooled, the dish is heated for 3 minutes on a boiling water bath. A violet-red colour indicates the presence of amyl alcohol; if there is a lot, the colour forms even without heating.

t: Amyl alcohol: amyl acetate and oxidation
n: The amyl acetate and oxidation reactions for amyl alcohol. For amyl acetate, 2 drops of concentrated H2SO4 and dried sodium acetate are added to the residue, which is heated gradually; an odour resembling pear essence is perceived. For oxidation, the residue is dissolved in ether; after the ether has evaporated, a few drops of 1% KMnO4 and an equal amount of concentrated H2SO4 are added, and the mixture is heated for 1-2 minutes on a water bath. First the pleasant odour of isovaleraldehyde is perceived, then the unpleasant odour of isovaleric acid, resembling rotten cheese.

The n-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde reaction for amyl alcohol. To the residue, 5-10 drops of a 0.5% solution of n-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde in H2SO4 are added. A dark red colour forms. If the mixture is diluted with water, the colour changes to violet.

The significance of ethylene glycol. Antifreeze consists of 55% ethylene glycol and 45% water, and does not freeze even at -40 °C. If it is drunk in place of an alcoholic drink, the patient suddenly loses consciousness; breathing is disturbed, convulsions occur, and the pupils dilate. An amount of 100 to 300 ml is fatal; 50 ml has a toxic effect on the body. Glycolic acid formed in its metabolism accumulates; it is oxidised to oxalic acid, combines with calcium and collects in the renal tubules.

The metabolism of ethylene glycol and its effect on the kidney. Ethylene glycol is rapidly absorbed through the intestine and rapidly metabolised by enzymes. The glycolic acid formed accumulates in the body, is oxidised to oxalic acid and combines with calcium. Calcium oxalate collects in the renal tubules and the vessels of the brain, endangering the function of these organs. About 3% is excreted unchanged.

Ethylene glycol poisoning is divided into stages. At first the person feels intoxicated, with pain in the lower back and abdomen, and then loses consciousness. In acute poisoning, tachycardia, tachypnoea and pulmonary oedema are observed during 12-24 hours. During 24-72 hours, renal failure and metabolic acidosis develop. The patient may die after 13-14 days from anuria. In the corpse, cerebral haemorrhage is found, and the renal passages are filled with calcium oxalate.

The properties and uses of ethylene glycol. Pure ethylene glycol is a colourless, oily-viscous, sweet-tasting, odourless, hygroscopic liquid; it boils at 197.0 °C, with a specific gravity of 1.127. Antifreeze consists of 55% ethylene glycol and 45% water, and does not freeze even at -40 °C. In engineering it is used as a lubricant, in hydraulic fluids and ink, and in making plastics and polyester fibres.

Ethylene glycol is isolated by the method of Lapkina and Nazarenko. The liver is taken for analysis, because ethylene glycol accumulates mainly in the liver. To 10 g of liver, 5 g of crystals of oxalic acid is added, and the mixture is ground in a porcelain mortar. It is transferred to a flask, 30 ml of benzene is added on top, and the mixture is boiled on a water bath. Then the aqueous layer is separated.

The identity reactions of ethylene glycol. A precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide dissolves, giving a clear blue liquid; glycerol interferes with this reaction. With potassium periodate in an acid medium, ethylene glycol is oxidised to formaldehyde, which is then detected by the characteristic reactions of formaldehyde. With concentrated nitric acid it is oxidised to oxalic acid; with ammonium hydroxide and calcium salts, a white precipitate of calcium oxalate forms. In GLC it is identified by its retention parameters.

The calcium oxalate reaction. If concentrated nitric acid is added to the extract 2-3 times and the mixture is heated, ethylene glycol is oxidised to oxalic acid. If ammonium hydroxide and calcium salts are added to the oxalic acid, a white precipitate of calcium oxalate forms. Under the microscope, envelope-shaped crystals are seen; they dissolve in mineral acids. The sensitivity of the reaction is 0.1 g of ethylene glycol.

Let us summarise the principal reactions for alcohols. Methyl alcohol forms an ester with salicylic acid and, on oxidation with permanganate, forms formaldehyde. For ethyl alcohol, the iodoform, isonitrile, acetaldehyde and ethyl acetate reactions are carried out. For amyl alcohol, the salicylaldehyde, amyl acetate and oxidation reactions are used. These reactions show the differences between the alcohols, but some of them have negative forensic chemical significance.

In the "Wheel" exercise we match reactions to alcohols. For methyl alcohol, the methyl salicylate reaction and oxidation with KMnO4 with detection of formaldehyde are carried out. For ethyl alcohol, the iodoform, isonitrile, acetaldehyde and ethyl acetate reactions are carried out. For amyl alcohol, the salicylaldehyde, amyl acetate, oxidation and n-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde reactions are used. Do not forget that the odour of methyl salicylate is similar to that of ethyl alcohol.

t: Case 6: road accident, blood and urine
n: Case 6: road accident, blood and urine. Samples of 10 ml of blood and 10 ml of urine from a person who had a car accident after drinking alcohol were brought to forensic chemical examination. More ethyl alcohol was found in the blood than in the urine. Task: explain the situation and carry out the forensic chemical analysis. In table form, record the type of problem, its causes and ways of resolving it.

The line of discussion for case 6. The case presents samples of 10 ml of blood and 10 ml of urine from a person who had a road accident after drinking alcohol. More ethyl alcohol was found in the blood than in the urine. In poisoning, the concentration of alcohol in the urine is considerably higher than in the blood; alcohol passes quickly into the blood and is rapidly oxidised in the liver. Ethyl alcohol is isolated by steam distillation and detected by the iodoform reaction, the ethyl acetate reaction and others. The quantity is found by the ethyl nitrite method, the Widmark-Shaymosh method or GLC, and then the concentrations in the blood and urine are compared.

The review questions are as follows. What is the toxicological and narcological significance of methyl, ethyl and amyl alcohols, and how are they isolated from a biological object? What are the reactions of methyl alcohol for ester formation with salicylic acid and for detection by oxidation? What are the reactions of ethyl alcohol for forming iodoform and isonitrile, and for forming the ethyl acetic and benzoic ethyl esters? How are the reaction of amyl alcohol with salicylaldehyde, detection by oxidation, formation of the acetic amyl ester and quantification of the alcohols carried out?

Safety and conclusion. The student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask to the laboratory work. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard, which are locked and sealed when the work is finished. Conclusion: for methyl alcohol, salicylate ester formation and oxidation are used; for ethyl alcohol, the iodoform, isonitrile and ethyl acetate reactions; for amyl alcohol, the salicylaldehyde, amyl acetate and oxidation reactions.
